content: Tocopherols are a group of chemical compounds, many of which exhibit vitamin E activity. These compounds are organic in nature and consist of various methylated phenols. The term tocopherol was coined in 1936 after the discovery of its role as a dietary fertility factor in rats. The name is derived from the Greek words τόκος (childbirth) and φέρειν (to bear), with the suffix -ol indicating its chemical classification as an alcohol. Tocotrienols, which are structurally related compounds, may also possess vitamin E activity. Collectively, all derivatives with vitamin E activity are referred to as vitamin E. Both tocopherols and tocotrienols are fat-soluble antioxidants. The compound α-tocopherol, a common form of tocopherol used in food products, is labeled with the E number E307. Natural vitamin E exists in eight distinct forms: four tocopherols and four tocotrienols. Each of these forms features a chromanol ring with a hydroxyl group capable of donating a hydrogen atom to neutralize free radicals, as well as a hydrophobic side chain that facilitates penetration into biological membranes. The tocopherols and tocotrienols are further classified into alpha, beta, gamma, and delta forms, based on the number of methyl groups on the chromanol ring. Each form exhibits slightly different biological activities. As a food additive, tocopherols are labeled with E numbers such as E307 (α-tocopherol), E308 (γ-tocopherol), and E309 (δ-tocopherol). Vitamin E capsules are sometimes used as visible markers in magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). Alpha-tocopherol is traditionally considered the most biologically active antioxidant form of vitamin E in humans. The measurement of vitamin E activity in international units (IU) was originally based on its ability to prevent spontaneous abortions in pregnant rats. During human pregnancies, α-tocopherol levels naturally increase by approximately 150% in maternal circulation. One IU of tocopherol is defined as ⅔ milligrams of RRR-α-tocopherol (formerly known as d-α-tocopherol). Alternatively, one IU is defined as 1 milligram of the 8-isomer mix all-rac-α-tocopheryl acetate (commercially referred to as dl-α-tocopheryl acetate). The original semi-synthetic molecular mix, known as 2-ambo-α-tocopherol, is no longer manufactured. Other RRR-tocopherol vitamins are gradually being recognized for their additional roles in human health as research progresses. Advocates of naturopathic and orthomolecular medicine recommend that vitamin E supplements contain at least 20% by weight of other natural vitamin E isomers. Tocotrienols, which also belong to the vitamin E family, consist of four d-isomers. These compounds share structural similarities with tocopherols but differ in having an unsaturated bond in each of the three isoprene units that form their hydrocarbon tail. In contrast, tocopherols have a saturated phytyl tail. The history of vitamin E began in 1922 when Herbert McLean Evans discovered an unknown vitamin necessary for fertility in rats. This condition was reversed by feeding the rats wheat germ. In 1936, the active substance was isolated from wheat germ, and its chemical formula (C29H50O2) was determined. Evans identified the compound as an alcohol due to its reaction properties and named it tocopherol. The structure of tocopherol was elucidated in 1938. The Recommended Daily Allowance (RDA) for vitamin E for a 25-year-old male is 15 mg/day, based on the α-tocopherol form due to its high biological activity. Surveys such as NHANES III (1988–91) and CSFII (1994) indicate that most Americans do not meet the recommended intake of vitamin E. However, the Institute of Medicine (IOM) suggests that these estimates may be low due to underreporting of dietary fat intake. The IOM also states that most North American adults obtain sufficient vitamin E from their diets but cautions individuals on low-fat diets to ensure adequate intake of α-tocopherol. Vitamin E supplements are best absorbed when taken with meals. Excessive vitamin E intake can act as an anticoagulant, increasing the risk of bleeding. Therefore, an upper tolerable intake level (UL) of 1,000 mg (1,500 IU) per day has been established. The richest dietary sources of vitamin E are vegetable oils such as palm oil, sunflower oil, corn oil, soybean oil, and olive oil. Other sources include nuts, sunflower seeds, seabuckthorn berries, kiwi fruit, wheat germ, whole grains, fish, peanut butter, goat's milk, and green leafy vegetables. Fortified breakfast cereals are also a significant source in the United States. While vitamin E was originally extracted from wheat germ oil, most natural supplements are now derived from vegetable oils, typically soybean oil. Vitamin E deficiency is rare but can occur in specific situations, such as in individuals with disorders of fat metabolism or very low birth weight infants. Deficiency is often characterized by neurological problems due to impaired nerve conduction. Conditions such as cystic fibrosis, Crohn's disease, liver disease, and pancreatic insufficiency may impair fat absorption, necessitating supplemental vitamin E. Abetalipoproteinemia, a rare inherited disorder of fat metabolism, can lead to severe vitamin E deficiency, causing symptoms like poor nerve impulse transmission, muscle weakness, and retinal degeneration. High-dose vitamin E supplementation can reverse these complications. Another rare genetic condition, isolated vitamin E deficiency, results from mutations in the tocopherol transfer protein gene and requires high-dose supplementation. Commercial vitamin E supplements are available in several forms, including fully synthetic dl-α-tocopherol, semi-synthetic natural source vitamin E esters, and less processed natural mixed tocopherols. Synthetic vitamin E, derived from petroleum products, is manufactured as all-rac-α-tocopheryl acetate, containing eight isomers, only one of which is biologically active. Natural α-tocopherol (RRR-α-tocopherol) is more biologically active than synthetic forms. Semi-synthetic vitamin E is produced by methylating other tocopherol isomers extracted from plant oils. These forms are often esterified for stability and ease of use in supplements. However, esterified forms are less efficiently absorbed in humans compared to rats. Tocopheryl esters are also used in cosmetics and pharmaceuticals. Vitamin E is widely used as a preservative in cosmetics and foods. It is believed to benefit the skin, but some individuals may experience allergic reactions to tocopheryl esters. Topical use of vitamin E for scar reduction has limited evidence of efficacy, with some studies showing no improvement or even adverse effects like contact dermatitis. Studies on vitamin E's role in preventing heart disease, cancer, cataracts, and age-related macular degeneration (AMD) have yielded mixed results. While observational studies suggest potential benefits, randomized clinical trials have not consistently demonstrated efficacy. For example, vitamin E supplementation has not been shown to reduce cardiovascular events or cancer incidence. In some cases, high-dose vitamin E supplementation has been associated with increased risks, such as heart failure or lung cancer in smokers. Further research is needed to clarify these findings and determine the optimal use of vitamin E in disease prevention.
